en: The Sūtra of Brief Exhortation Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Command.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada.
At the Jeta Grove, together with an immeasurable assembly of bhikṣus,
the Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!"

Within my Dharma, there is the practice of living with few desires and knowing contentment; that is to say, my disciples shave their heads, don dyed robes, carry alms bowls, and go from house to house to beg for food to sustain themselves—an act held in contempt by the foolish of the world.

If there is a son of good family with pure faith who leaves the household life for homelessness and practices this matter—not out of being oppressed by royal difficulties, nor out of fear of thieves, debt, alarm, or the inability to survive, but solely out of having resolved his mind to cultivate weariness toward birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; desiring to sever the mass of suffering and the fetters of the afflictions, to reach their ultimate end, and to seek liberation—[then he shall attain it].
"Is it not for this very purpose that you have sought to go forth?
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"So it is, so it is! It is for the sake of liberation that one seeks to go forth. "O bhikṣus!"

Suppose there is a certain class of sinful bhikṣus who, despite having left the household life, are by nature full of greed and defilement; they develop deep attachment toward the objects of the five desires, or give rise to anger and evil thoughts. Their minds are constantly dissipated and they lack diligent exertion; they are always full of delusive thoughts and do not practice the gates of concentration. Clinging to various sensory objects, they delight in inferior matters and do not aspire to superior practices, and thus they ultimately achieve nothing.
What is this evil person like?
O bhikṣus, listen to a parable.
It is like a corpse-wood burning in a wild field, scorched at both ends and filthy in the middle; this wood is unfit for use by either people of the village or people of the wild fields.
I now employ this analogy for those certain types of monastics who are indolent and deluded;

having abandoned the various pleasures of the secular world, yet failing to cultivate the goals and benefits of a śramaṇa, they constantly give rise to three kinds of unwholesome thoughts: namely, thoughts of the five desires, thoughts of malice and harm, and thoughts of deception.
From what do these three kinds of unwholesome thoughts arise?
One should know that they all originate with ignorance as their cause; at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, one falls into the three evil destinies.
Therefore, you should diligently practice and sever ignorance.
I am the Great Teacher and you are my disciples; I shall now explain for you the essential and concise matters within my teaching.
Out of great compassion, out of pity, for the sake of benefit, and for the sake of supreme happiness, you should practice as I have taught.
Whether you are in the mountains, forests, hermitages, under trees, or in the open air, you should reflect well and not be negligent; do not let regret arise in your mind at a later time!
"By practicing as taught, you shall attain liberation.
When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, the assembly of bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus ends the *Sūtra of Brief Exhortation* spoken by the Buddha.
